utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Indic, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Mr. Indic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday we broke off at the question of verbal protests, and what you would do once you received a verbal protest. You said that following the reception of a verbal protest, you would try and see the situation. Can I first ask you, who would you first do this with, to look if the protest was complete?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that there were norms, standards, accepted what a protest would have to include so that it can then be reacted upon, every member of our group was able to assess whether all the elements necessary -- necessary elements were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that there were norms, standards, according to which it was possible to assess whether a protest was complete. Could you tell us what would that include according to you? What were these norms, according to which you would assess that it was a standard -- complete protest?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to react properly, adequately, upon a protest, it was necessary for the protest to include the time, the location, the area of firing or a direction of firing if it was firing or an operation. Whenever it was possible, it would need to include the type of weapon that was fired and the consequences of the firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've told us the six elements that were necessary to satisfy a norm, that is, you say existed in terms of the contents or the completeness of the protest, can you tell us of those elements, that is, the time, location, the area, the direction of firing, the type of weapon, and the consequences, which one of these elements were included in a protest that you received?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, the protests were incomplete, and they had some general data given. For instance, it wouldn't include the exact time. For instance, it would say in the course of yesterday, there was firing in the area of Marin Dvor. Those kind of protests was useless. And nothing can be taken, no measures can be taken if the protest remains in this form.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So once you've told us that you needed to look at the complete picture of the protest, and now you've told us what a protest would look like, the one that you received, what steps would you then take to receive information in order to see the whole picture of the protest? Who would do that? Who would take the steps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that the protest doesn't remain just a formal matter, but it actually -- something can be done, some measures can be taken following the protest, the first thing we would do is that those who would give the protest to us directly and in a specific case, those would be the military observers of the United Nations, we would then ask from them to give additional supplemental information to the protest, as much as they were able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you would ask from UN members who would be addressing protests to you once you've asked them to add additional information, could you tell us what kind of responses did you receive from UN members? In a sense, what kind of return information did you receive in order to complete the protest?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems incredible, but following our requests, we never received any additional information in relation to these protests. And so, we believed that then the opposing side, which had put in the formal protest through the UN, had either decided not to lodge any protest or that simply there was no reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were two reasons, either that the protest wasn't real or that there was a misinformation. Can you tell us, in what sense would that have been misinformation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that in some cases, communication systems of the UN and of the instance of protests which went through the UN military observers would be used to misinform the enemy, the opponent. I state this because occasionally, we used this instance in order to misinform the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, can you tell us, in your opinion, UN officers -- first of all, in your opinion, were they aware of the disposition of positions of the BH army and the Army of Republika Srpska? And if they were, to what extent were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to assess the level of expertise of UN members who were deployed in our areas. I don't want to be unfair. But I have to say that their number as well as the mandate for their mission, it reflected negatively on their possibility to see the situation of the front and the daily events on both sides of the front line. Not just to see that situation, but also to understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, when you were telling us about the completeness of protests, you told us that you wanted some return information and that protests were very frequently incomplete. Can you tell us if there were any cases in which you would receive protests where you had some elements on the basis of which you were able to check and, as you said, react through the duty officer to the protest received? What was it that the duty officer was able to do if the protest did include time, location, and the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A series of protests were received that we were able to handle timely, and I really have to stress the word "timely," in timely fashion. These were protests that we received directly from military observers during the time while combat operations were ongoing. Those kind of protests were then simultaneously addressed from the command of the military observers to the command of the Sarajevo sector to both sides. Once such a protest arrived with the request to stop firing, we would then take this protest to the duty operations officer at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the duty operations officer at the corps command, what steps would he take -- what steps was he able to take in order to react on a protest that he received?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In coordination with representative of our group, the duty operations officer would call the brigade commander from the area of responsibility in question, the one that was listed as where firing operations were ongoing, first of all, in order to check the authenticity of the protest received and to see what really was going on on the ground. As I've already said, mostly these were combat operations on both sides, mutual combat operations, following a desire that was expressed to stop the firing operations by both sides, military observers would then mediate in order to establish the exact time when the firing or the operations would stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that the duty operations officer would forward the protest to the brigade commander in whose area of responsibility there were operations of firing according to the information received, can you tell us if the brigade commander had the obligation to give a return information upon the protest received, if this -- if there was firing or operations in his area of responsibility to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this has not been put in the best possibly military vocabulary. The duty operations officer does not forward this to the brigade commander, but he asks from the brigade commander a kind of interim combat report to find out what's really happening in the area of responsibility of his brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So if I've understood you correctly, the brigade commander does submit a report to the duty officer what's happening in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The brigade commander has to reply to the duty officer and say what's happening in his area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally have information or knowledge if such checks occurred? What were brigade commanders informing the duty officer or you, considering that your group received the protests? Did you then tell the UN, inform the UN, that you did carry out the check, and what information was received?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that we respected the principle that there was a return information to those who had lodged a protest, in this case, that would be UN military observers, throughout the procedure, we would follow what the duty officer was doing. And as much as this was necessary, we would inform the military observers of the UN about the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You now told us what the protest would be like, for instance, during the course of yesterday, there was firing or operation in such and such an area and there was firing. On any occasion, do you recall that you received a protest saying that SRK forces were firing with snipers or did the protest say they were using infantry weapons? So in the sense of such a definition, did you receive either one or the other or both?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is interesting that it seems that in the area of SRK, there was no waging war with infantry weapons because what term was used, that all types of infantry weapons were called snipers. And that's how the protests were written. Whenever infantry weapons were fired, then in the protests, there would be mention of sniper activity, sniper firing. It seems absurd, but according to the protests, a sniper could even use a burst mode.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, do you recall if you have ever in your group for cooperation while you worked as a liaison officer, did you receive a protest in a sense as you've said, with the time, with the location, with the direction of firing, and type of weapon, and that in that protest is said as a consequence, such and such a number of people were killed or this person was killed specifically? Do you -- did you receive these kind of protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decisively, I say that I have never received protest in this form.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were speaking about the protests, you said that also the Serb side lodged protests through the UN military observers, and I believe you also said through liaison officers within which was the liaison officer for battalions. Can you tell us what were the protests like that you lodged in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One feature of the protests that were sent by our side was that they were not so numerous for the simple reason that there was a natural characteristic that Serbs do not want to complain a great deal to someone else about their own problems. Most frequently protests by our side were lodged at the time when cease-fires had been signed and agreed because there were violations of cease-fires by the Muslim side, either by opening fire or by engineering works or by regrouping their forces and their equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, can you tell us, if you recall, that in the course of your service you've ever received a protest that in a certain part of town, there was an incident that occurred when many civilians -- where many civilians were killed and that it was specified when and where this occurred, in which part of the city under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive this kind of protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, you said that apart from verbal protest, you also received written protests. Can you tell us, what were the conditions usually that these protests arrived in? That is, the reasons when these written protests arrived.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Written protests were mostly related to cease-fire violations in the period when such cease-fires were signed and agreed, and the protests were sent, as I've already told you, simultaneously to both sides. The second kind of written protests were protests that were sent if for any reason there was a threat that existed for a UN unit or UN members.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, according to your recollection, how many such written protests did you receive and what was the reason -- what was written? In fact, you did say that was mostly because of cease-fire violations. But can you recall how many of such written protests there were and what would you do then upon receipt of such written protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say numerically how many such written protests were received, but I can say more or less that it was about 50, 50 or so, as far as I was able to see. Upon receipt of a written protest, my obligation, my duty, was to forward this protest to the corps commander because it is always addressed to the corps commander, or if he was absent, this would be forwarded to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you have any knowledge or information whether the content of the protest was checked, and did you reply in writing to such protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the commander would do specifically after receiving a protest. But it was always personally either the commander or the chief of staff who would write a response to that protest, and that would be given to our group, which would translate it and then send it to whoever had addressed it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, the reference to the number of written protests, could that be clarified in terms of what period of time. I don't think that has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, though I think you could have asked it in cross-examination. But since you interrupted anyhow. You said there were approximately 50 written protests. During what period of time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understood that we were talking here about the relevant period, while General Galic was the corps commander, and that was how I gave my answer in relation to that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're talking about September 1992 to August 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm talking about this period. And I have to stress that the number of 50, I've used it as an approximate approximation, not as a precise number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that you translated the contents of the responses to those protests and that you sent them back from the person or the instance that had sent out the protest in the first place, bearing that in mind, can you tell us if the corps command ever lodged any protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A moment ago, I think I mentioned that it was in particular during the periods of time that were subject to cease-fire agreements. Those protests were usually related to cease-fire violations in any form or shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is in the possession of a document which it had already disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with your permission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- You always indicate it was disclosed. The Chamber expects that any document you show to a witness that it has been disclosed. And please inform us if it has not been disclosed. Mr. Usher, could you...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's for the benefit of my colleagues, Your Honour, that I say that because this is a document that will be also produced later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's D1840. Mr. Indic, do you have D1840 of the 21st of April, 1994 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, can you recognise this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is a protest that was sent by the SRK command to the UNPROFOR command. The addressee -- the addressees were commanders Rose and Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, something about the contents of this particular protest.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is about a failure to comply with the cease-fire on the part of Muslims, and the protest specifies a number of such incidents, a number of incidents where the cease-fire was violated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read for us item number 2 of this document, Mr. Indic, please. It starts with the words "the most characteristic examples..."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The most characteristic examples of serious violations of cease-fire are the following: During the whole day have infantry fire over positions of the region in Okruglica."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the remaining items also briefly specify the area where infantry fire was opened from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the remaining points make mention of the type of fire, where it came from, and what areas on our side were targeted. And at the end, the protest also specifies the consequences including one fatality and several incidents of wounding. Six seriously wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, can you tell us if this protest that you now see in front of you was signed by Brigadier General Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Galic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your recollection, can you tell us whether at the time you lodged these written protests, whether you ever received answers, responses, to your written protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The written protests which were lodged in this form to the UNPROFOR command were never given any response.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, you said that this was just a kind of written protest that was sent from the corps command. I should like to know how often this type of protests were sent to the UNPROFOR command, if you remember. And tell us, please, if you ever received any response to such written protests.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already indicated that the protests were mostly lodged during the cease-fire, whenever the cease-fire was severely violated by the Muslim side. Very often, these protests were just a compilation of reports on cease-fire violations. And, I repeat, we never received any response to any of these protests.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you told us about written protests that were sent to the sector commander or UNPROFOR command, can you describe for us the cooperation with UNPROFOR members during the relevant period of times, that is, between the time when General Galic took office and the time he left? Do you have any knowledge as to how often any meetings took place with UNPROFOR, and what were the results of such cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me begin with the easy part: That is, how often this cooperation took place. If we were to assess it in view of the number of meetings held, then I can say that it was very successful. I would even venture and say that there were more meetings than it was actually necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, let us be more precise. You told us that there had been more meetings than necessary. What exactly did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am referring, first of all, to the meetings that General Galic as a corps commander held with UNPROFOR representatives. Wishing to make a significant contribution on his behalf, he very often held meetings with officers who held significantly lower rank in terms of military hierarchy than he did. As a corps commander, he never refused to have a meeting with a battalion commander of UNPROFOR, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about the meetings that General Galic held with lower ranking officers, because of his willingness to cooperate as best as he could with UNPROFOR members, you mentioned the fact that he even held -- had meetings with battalion commanders. Do you personally know what battalion commanders the General met with during the relevant times? And if you do, if you happened to be present at such meetings, do you know what issues were discussed during such encounters?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, UNPROFOR had four battalions, two French battalions, one Ukrainian battalion, and one Egyptian battalion. As far as I know, General Galic never met with the Egyptian battalion commander. He was the only battalion commander that he didn't meet with because he never requested such a meeting. As for the commanders of the remaining three battalions, such meetings were held almost regularly. As for the particular commanders, it's difficult to say because they rotated every six months. I can perhaps mention some names, Sartre, Poulet, De Kermabon [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present at any such meeting with battalion commanders? And if yes, do you remember any subject that was discussed with battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would usually attend such meetings for the purposes of organisation of such meetings and also in order to translate. The agenda usually focussed on the specific mission of the battalion in question. If, for instance, we were meeting with the French battalion, whose members were tasked with guarding the airport, providing security at the airport, then we would usually talk about the problems concerning the airport. Humanitarian missions were also on the agenda, such as the situation with the needs of the population in the given area and the ability of UN members to help if any such help was requested. The issues of various types of repair work and maintenance and so on and so forth. Of course, we would always exchange opinions as to how to achieve a cessation of hostilities and to create appropriate conditions for the politicians to end the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you do remember these meetings, and you attended them and you told us about the agenda of such meetings. Tell us, please, do you remember, at any such meeting held with battalion commanders, do you remember any complaints being -- having been voiced by such battalion commanders in their discussions with the General to the effect that members of the SRK and your services were not cooperative, were not acting upon the protests, and were refusing to work with them? Do you remember any such discussions having taken place during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such assessments were ever made. Quite the contrary: Full satisfaction was often expressed by all members of the UN. With the level of cooperation that they were receiving from our side. They even went so far as to openly declare that whenever they attended, they had a meeting with our side, it was almost like a rest for them, that they were resting during such meetings. There were comments from time to time made to that effect, but they never resulted in any verbal conflict during such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, in view of the fact that you attended some of these meetings, both in your capacity as a liaison officer and an interpreter, can you tell us whether any other interpreters were ever present at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN members who came to these meetings would usually come with their interpreters who were local residents employed with the UN. However, because of the fact that local employees were almost a hundred per cent from the Muslim-controlled territory, we could not fully trust their objectivity and professionalism when interpreting. So it was necessary for someone from the group to be present at such meetings if nothing for the purpose of controlling the accuracy of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said, Mr. Indic, that the General, wishing to overcome all the problems in the SRK area of responsibility, also accepted meetings with battalion commanders that you yourself attended, can you tell us approximately the number of such meetings that you also attended?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the number of the battalions in question that I already mentioned, such a meeting would be held at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We have dealt with the issue of meetings with battalion commanders. Can you tell us if there were any meetings at a higher level between General Galic and sector commanders? And if so, did you attend any of these, and tell us also how frequently they were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such meetings were held when necessary, that is, whenever it was necessary, the corps commander and the Sarajevo sector commander would meet together. On an average, such meetings took place every 15 or 20 days. But they could also be held more frequently. Sometimes several -- on several days in a row. If it was necessary to achieve -- to reach an agreement on a more significant issue. The reason behind it being the fact that the sector command had to act simultaneously with other commanders and hold a meeting on the same day in the Lukavica building and at the 1st Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, these meetings that were held frequently, as you said, and you indicated how frequent they were, did they result in any report being submitted to the chief of staff? Were contents of these meetings subject to any daily reports of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an obligation of the corps command to inform the main staff on the regular activities of the UN forces in the area of responsibility of the corps. In addition to these regular reports, whenever a meeting was held or whenever it was necessary to obtain the opinion of the main staff concerning certain issues, special reports would also be sent out. To conclude, the main staff was familiar with all the meetings that the corps command held at its level with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence would like to show three documents to Mr. Indic. D467, 560, and 561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, these documents, were they recently disclosed or were they disclosed at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At an earlier stage, Your Honour. The documents were on the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, would you be so kind and place the document on the ELMO, please, so that we can all see it. 467, please. Let's have that one, first. You can just put it on the ELMO. Mr. Indic, do you have in front of you 467?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If it is easier for you, you can perhaps proceed with telling us if the document is dated the 21st of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a regular combat report with a situation at 1700 sent out to the VRS main staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In item number 5 of this document -- do you see a number 5?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does it speak about the state of security and morale and the control points under UNPROFOR's control and the deployment of the Russian battalion that arrived at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this document signed by General Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, would you now please have a look at Document Number 560. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a regular combat report of the SRK command sent to the VRS main staff dated the 30th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In this document under item 3, section (b), we read the words "activity of UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated that a meeting was held between General Galic and General Soubirou, and the schedule, the agenda of the meeting, is also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The agenda being the usage of blue roads, the freedom of movement, and the accommodation of new UNPROFOR units, and problems regarding weapon collection, sites for grouping of our weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, once again, is this document signed by General Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Document 561, please, Mr. Indic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a regular combat report of the SRK command sent to the VRS main staff on the 31st of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 3, does this regular combat report describe the situation on the territory, and under item (a) activities of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it states that a meeting was held between SRK commander and Major General Kuksenko, UN liaison officer for the area of former Yugoslavia and a commander of the Ukraine battalion in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, in item 2 of item 3, it says that women and children had blocked the road in Hadzici, and that the French convoy of UNPROFOR was currently on the blockade as well as several vehicles of UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this document also signed by Major-General Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that I've shown you these three documents as three regular daily reports and we saw that under item 3 of the documents 561 and 560, there was an item entitled "UNPROFOR activity" and also in the other document, although it was a different item. Could you tell us whether in the regular daily reports, this was the type and the content -- the form and the content of reporting as far as UNPROFOR activities are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reporting on UNPROFOR activities in daily combat reports was an obligatory item.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, after we have read Document 560 where it's reported that there was a meeting held between Major-General Galic and General Soubirou, and we saw that the agenda of meeting was use of blue roads, freedom of movement, accommodation of new UNPROFOR units and problems regarding the weapons collection sites, can you tell us, when you attended these meetings, and if you did attend such meetings, apart from such items on the agenda, was there any talk, any discussions, related to problems of shelling and infantry fire or, as you say, it was usual to put sniping fire on protests? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that at such meetings, there was talk both on opening fire in cases when combat operations were ongoing, and there was an attempt or there were attempts by UNPROFOR command to talk with both sides and ensure that conditions are established to have a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if those meetings, when certain problems were resolved in the area of responsibility of the corps and when sector commander was present, these issues which were a problem and that were on the agenda, when these issues were dealt with, what was the cooperation like of the corps command? Specifically we're talking about when freedom of movement was concerned and humanitarian aid, and also the use of blue roads. So basically, what was the cooperation of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and of the general when it was necessary to deal and resolve certain problems?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic was always and expressed his readiness to resolve every problem in a constructive manner. I assessed that UNPROFOR members had a high regard for the degree of cooperation, judging this on the fact that there was never a single remark -- there was never a criticism of the level of cooperation of the cooperation given -- offered by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, if you recall in the document 561, item 3, paragraph of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... To the witness. It's 561.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, you read it under item 3, paragraph 2 that women and children had blocked the road in Hadzici, and that there was a blocked French UNPROFOR convoy as well as some UNMOs' vehicles. Do you have any knowledge about this incident, personal knowledge of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall this extremely well. I recall the incident well. And unfortunately, it wasn't the only one that happened. The problem of the road blockade in Hadzici was caused by unsuccessful negotiations with the Muslim side to release prisoners in prisons, Serb civilians from the prison in Tarcin whose families were in Hadzici. The road blockade in Hadzici was done by wives, mothers, and children of those imprisoned civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether this problem was successfully resolved? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the prison in Tarcin for which I have to express that it contained only civilians was one of the last prisons in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina that was closed down. And it was always used by the Muslim side to have a group of hostages which were used in various ways during negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Indic, you told us at some point that there were meetings held at the corps command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, are you finished with the documents because in order to prevent that we have to put it back. I would have one additional question. Would you please, Mr. Indic, look at these documents, the document that is in front of you. You see that at the top, and that's the same for all the three documents, you find a stamp which is a stamp related to these proceedings. But there's also some handwriting on it. It seems to start with "ST.POV" or ROV, and then a number and then a date. Was that on these documents at that time as well, or has this been added later as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this writing in the top right corner is exactly the same as what's in the left corner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I mean handwriting at the top. Could you please point at it so that we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was later put in. It wasn't in the original document. The only thing that was done was to copy the number of the documents into which it was entered in a log book. It was just to copy it on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the handwriting is -- that was put on it when it was stored or have you any -- could you explain what it means, the handwriting on the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. This is not my handwriting. It wasn't added in by me. But perhaps if the document was sent anywhere by fax, and if the number could not be seen very well on the document itself, perhaps it was added in black pen so that it could be seen on the fax. Because the number is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What number is the same? I see that the date is the same. I see that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Date is the same and the number is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I see. And these numbers, were they -- would every new document get the next number, or was there any system in that? Because I noticed that the document related to the 30th of March bears the number 15.1.92. Whereas the document of the 31st of March bears the number 15.1.93. Are these subsequent numbers for these kind of reports, or could you explain what the number exactly is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what was the principle of registering, logging operation of documentation, so I'm afraid I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, you were telling us about morning meetings that were held at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you personally or someone on behalf of a group for cooperation attended such morning meetings. And if you have, how frequently was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, there were two types of morning meetings. When there were intense combat operations on the ground, meetings were held of only the core command, C-O-R-E command, at which the representative of the UNPROFOR cooperation group was not present. If the situation was normal, so to speak, there were extended meetings of the core command, and then also the chief of the UNPROFOR cooperation group was also present. In the first part of the meeting which was in relation to reporting and telling about the problems in the second part of the meeting when the commander would issue, give orders for that day, then the chief of the group, cooperation group, was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, could you tell us if you know whether at such meetings, brigade commanders were also present?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, brigade commanders did not attend meetings at the corps command, only in cases when there were some biannual analysis meetings or annual analysis meetings or when orders were issued that were of general character and that related to the entire structure of the corps command, then brigade commanders would attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, can you tell us whether you know, whether you're aware of the existence of a standing, of a permanent order by General Galic issued to brigade commanders about the duties, activities, obligations in relation to artillery use, mortar use when enemy positions are fired on? Do you have any knowledge about the contents of such orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that liaison officers were not part of that system of the chain of command, of the command and control, the orders that went to the brigade commanders, that is something that remained unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you, as a corps member, did you know whether there was a rule about brigade deployment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every brigade worked based on the rules for brigade deployment. That is an official document. It's instructions, rules, regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that every brigade worked on the basis of rules for brigade deployment, did the brigade commander -- considering that such rules existed in certain situations, when a brigade commander would have to make a decision as to firing at a certain moment, did he need a separate order by the corps command? We're speaking about the brigade commander in the area of responsibility of his brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the rules, it is clearly specified when a unit can open fire without the order of the superior command. These were situations when the troops are under attack or facilities that this unit has in possession, when there is an activity which is directly threatening the lives of troops, and when the neighbouring unit is under attack. Even each individual as a soldier must not wait for an order to open fire if he has been attacked personally or the facility that he is protecting or his neighbour on the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at your answer, in view of the brigade commander's behaviour and the orders, did the brigade commander, if in the area of responsibility of his brigade under his command, if there was a need to open fire or to conduct operations or, if you say, another brigade was attacked, did the brigade commander need or have to inform the corps command if he did open fire, if he was to open fire?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the obligation duty of every commander to report to the superior command about the opening of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The contents of such report submitted by the brigade commander, when it was received by the corps, this report, did it go to the duty operations officer, and was it included in the report to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat the same answer as before: As a liaison officer, I was not within the system of the control and command to have access to the reports that the brigade sent to the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, can you tell us, what was the professional personnel of the corps command after the corps command was established? That is, at which level were members of the command personnel trained and also the commanders of the subordinate units, lower units?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, speaking about the established structure, it wasn't professionally trained, but the manpower, they were professionally trained, speaking about the officers that used to belong to the former JNA. The professionalism existed also on the level of brigade commanders. But the problem occurred below that level when because there was not a sufficient number of professional officers, battalion commands and those of lower units, they were staffed by persons who were not professional officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you arrived in Lukavica in September 1992. You told us that you attended morning meetings. Can you tell us whether at any point during those meetings that you attended, was there any talk of the objective of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time of my arrival at Lukavica, I never heard at any meeting in terms of an objective of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, at any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, can you tell us, bearing in mind the time that you've spent in the corps, you personally, can you tell us what was the objective?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, as a qualified, educated officer, there was no -- a strictly defined objective of the corps because in the area, there was an interspersing of various military and political interests, not only interests of the warring sides but much further afield. And all the activities that were ongoing in the area, from all that, it could be concluded undoubtedly that the main objective, the main aim of the corps was to preserve the established front lines in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the main aim was to preserve the established front lines in Sarajevo, can you tell us in your opinion when were these front lines established?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will probably be the first one who's going to say that these front lines in terms of people's minds were established at the time when there was a conflict in Croatia, from 1991. Anyone who wanted to see was able to see that Bosnia and Herzegovina was going to face civil war. When the first hostilities occurred, the so-called barricades were set up in some areas of Sarajevo. And in fact, these barricades ethnically demarcated areas of Sarajevo. With slight corrections, this line remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, you told us yesterday that in September 1992, you were forced to leave the PTT building because there was a physical threat to you and to your associate, that you were threatened with being killed personally by a Sarajevo criminal known as a Krusko?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Krusko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the existence of units that were led by certain persons who had a criminal record? Do you know anything about that, considering that you had lived in Sarajevo and that you were born there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very beginning of the war, it was allowed for the leading role in war to be taken up by criminals, first of all, by Juka Prazina, by Musan Topalovic, also known as Caco, by Cele 1, by Cele 2, Tope, and similar other persons. I can't even remember their nicknames now. And information regarding these groups, they can be gained through everyday conversations as well as by talking to UN members because of the problems they encountered when they met or when they had to deal with such groups. And also, by talking to people who managed somehow to leave the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control, and they were exposed -- they had been exposed to various unpleasant things and harassment while they were in that part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know whether these units were under the control of the BH army? And if they were, from what time? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not something connected to my area of activities, so these specific, precise details about placing such units under the control, I don't know these details. I personally believe that these kind of paramilitary units existed throughout the war under the area of Muslim -- in the area of Sarajevo under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it is now time for a break. And after the break, it is my co-counsel who will use the time that's still available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to address one matter very briefly for the parties. The Defence is informed about a letter of the Canadian authorities the senior legal officer has received. The Chamber understands a response to that letter will be given by the Defence itself, being the primarily responsible party for the subject matter of examination of witnesses. So therefore, the senior legal officer will be instructed to send a letter to the authorities indicating that they will receive a direct answer from you, and at the same time the Chamber will stress the importance of the appearance of Defence witnesses, and that if there would be any security concerns, that the Chamber would be glad to assist in resolving them. So that's the situation. I take it that this is -- yes. Then, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, with the examination of -- if possible, if we could possibly conclude the examination-in-chief by the next break, that would be fine. Then you would still have 10 minutes left, but if you would manage to do it in 5 minutes less --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. To the extent it is possible, I should be grateful if you could answer with yes or no. You spoke about some military units. Do you remember this? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us focus on paramilitary units on the Serb side. Can you briefly tell this Chamber if there were any difficulties to control the phenomena, and second, what were the measures taken in order to reduce or suppress these paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, there existed a number of paramilitary groups in the area of the SRK, as well. When I say "paramilitary group," in order to be precise, I have to tell you that I'm referring to the groups which did not respect the command and control system. As for the specific measures that the corps command undertook in order to place these groups under control, I'm afraid I cannot say anything precisely, but I know that in the first half of 1993, these groups were entirely disbanded, and their troops deployed in other units. However, the paramilitary issue was not fully resolved by the mere disbanding of these groups, in my opinion, because even a single individual who acts contrary to the orders of his superior commander on his own initiative, independently, can to a certain extent be considered as paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The group by the name of St. George, does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Vojvoda Brana group, does it sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must correct you. You probably wanted to say Vojvoda Brne.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You're quite correct, I apologise. Vojvoda Brne, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the paramilitary groups which was located at the Rakovica/Blazuj location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What specific measures or sanctions were taken in that respect, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What measures, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a military police unit was dispatched with the task of disbanding the said group. They were allowed to use force if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will see a video in a second. But in order to save time, with the assistance of Mr. Usher, let us distribute documents. But I will tell you when we will read this document and view the video later on. But let us have them distributed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In the meantime, I should like to ask several other questions, in particular concerning agreements. Witness, do you know whether the Serb side wanted to sign as many agreements as possible with the opposing side in order to achieve peace?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our commitment from the very beginning that a total cessation of hostilities should take place, not only in the area of the SRK but also in the entire territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I understand, your answer was given in affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in respect of the airport area, do you know whether there were any such agreements and whether it was the will and the willingness of the Serb side to have such agreements reached and whether they were indeed implemented in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1992, as far as the political level is concerned, and I believe it was Mr. Nikola Koljevic who signed the agreement, it was agreed that the airport should be taken over by UNPROFOR. According to this agreement, Serb forces withdrew from the airport, and the full control and the usage of the airport for humanitarian purposes was taken over by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You make mention of humanitarian purposes. In relation to this or these agreements, what happened with the issue of civilians and their transit over the airport area and their security? How was this problem treated in the agreements?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo airport agreement provided for an exclusive use of the airport for the purposes of humanitarian aid, the bringing in of the humanitarian aid, for the use by the UN and official delegations, which means that in the original of the agreement, the Sarajevo airport was not supposed to be used for civilians or any other categories of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what can you tell us about a willingness to demilitarise the corps, that is, the Serb side, if there was such willingness indeed during that period of time, which was designed to bring about peace?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the English booth, to demilitarise Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The willingness and efforts made in order to demilitarise Sarajevo were part of the overall attempt to bring about the cessation of hostilities throughout the area. Let me give you a specific example of these efforts made to demilitarise Sarajevo. A delegation of the VRS made an offer during these negotiations, that is, the negotiations of demilitarisation of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you personally take part in these meetings, that's my first question, and can you tell us when in period these meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as your first question, I attended personally most of these meetings. The second question, I'm not quite sure as to what you mean when you say "during that period."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The negotiations concerning a possible demilitarisation of Sarajevo, when did they take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the meetings generally speaking, then they were held from the outbreak of the hostilities until the very end of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Speaking of General Galic, did he attend these meetings? And if yes, what was his attitude towards this problem?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Galic did not attend the meetings of the mixed working group which were held at the Sarajevo airport. However, from the discussions that we had at the corps command, I know that everyone, including General Galic, supported the plan of the demilitarisation of Sarajevo which would have -- which was designed to bring about the cessation of hostilities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Still on the issue of demilitarisation of Sarajevo and its surroundings, what was the reaction of the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion, and judging from what could be seen, the Muslim side did not wish to accept this proposal. I think this was so because by demilitarising Sarajevo, they would have lost their political interest. When it comes to the allies, their allies, the allies of the Muslim side which in final conclusion would lead to their loss of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let us expand on this: You told us there was a political interest, namely that the international community would no longer be involved, and that the perception of the Muslim side was such that they thought that in the end, they would lose the war if they accepted the proposal. How did you reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before NATO interfered as a side in the conflict, the Serb side had under its control about 70 per cent of the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. With the loss of Sarajevo as the capital of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina, the war would soon end. And the result of the war would have been that the -- that the majority -- the largest part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have remained under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about 70 per cent of the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question is as follows: Before the war, who constituted majority in this area? I mean in terms of population strictly speaking or in terms of land ownership, that is, according to information that could be provided by the land survey office?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot answer your question because it requires a certain amount of professional expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you cannot tell us anything about it, neither in terms of territory or in terms of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are discussing political issues, I think this would be a convenient time for viewing the video. However, I have to say before we proceed that the document that we distributed a moment ago and that you have in front of you is merely an excerpt of a larger document. We copied pages 86 to 90, because they concern the video in question. Should you need the entire document, it can be obtained. But we didn't think it necessary to make such a large amount of copies for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what's going to happen, do I understand you well what we are going to see is an interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then are you asking questions about the subject of what is in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it not be the proper way of proceeding first to ask the witness what he knows about it before confronting him with the answers of the interviewed person, which would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, gladly. But I'm waiting for the answer. But I can, of course, do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the Prosecution would say -- I've got no idea. I haven't read the document. I haven't seen the interview. But in general terms, I would say it's always the proper way of first asking the witness and then confronting him with the views of someone else. But if the Prosecution would not object, knowing what is the interview about and knowing the transcript, then, of course, we might do it a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I make an observation in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Indic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence -- perhaps I could say this in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll then turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you please now talk about the problems of shooting, that is, shooting by the Muslim side. First question: Do you know anything about the group called Seva? Do you know anything about that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name of Mr. Edin Garaplija? Does this name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in a nutshell, what was this group Seva as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to information I have, the Seva group was a special unit, and they had the purpose of carrying out special tasks. They were mostly armed with sniper weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you mean by "special tasks"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under special tasks, first of all, I mean by eliminating persons, killing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, the witness should be asked the source of this information. "Do you know" is as far as we have got in that regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do I have to do it now or can I do it at the end of this exercise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's for the understanding of the Chamber, it might be better to learn about the basis of the knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us now very briefly where do you have this information? How did you come by it? How did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the initial information about the Seva group, I got at meetings of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps during their reporting by organs of intelligence and security matters. And this organ gave the first information about the existence of this group. Further information about the Seva group --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you now. When was it that you had the initial information given by the secret services in terms of year and month? Do you know when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely what month that was, but I can tell you it was the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other information, other bits of information about the Seva group I received through informal interviews with United Nations members, and most of the information that I received about the Seva group I received after the ending of the war by following the media on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the question was clarified. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to know one thing more. You told us about informal interviews with UN people, as far as I understood. Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on a daily basis for various reasons that UN members came to my offices. They were either military observers or people from the sector Sarajevo command or people from UNPROFOR. So there were many talks that we had. They were informal talks and interviews about the situation in Sarajevo and what was happening. It was through these discussions that I came to know about killing of civilians in Sarajevo and what was said in Sarajevo, that this was done, that these people were victims who were killed by the special units called Seva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have two more questions in this respect. First of all, you said that you know Mr. Garaplija. How did you meet him or how did you get to know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that I knew Mr. Garaplija personally, but that I knew of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about Mr. Garaplija from the media after he was arrested and detained in Zenica prison following the Pogorelica affair, that is, after the international community members burst into the camp for training of Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see a videotaped interview with Mr. Garaplija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I read an interview with Mr. Garaplija in Slobodna Bosna magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever read a transcript of an interview with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now here, before me, I can see a document when it was handed to me, part of the transcript where Mr. Garaplija was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my question is whether you ever read that transcript before --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the first time you see it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First time. First time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just to continue with the same line of questioning, Witness, the UN officials, did they tell you about the impression that they had in relation to shooting that may have happened and shooting that they were the targets of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean "an impression"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will rephrase. If you talked with UN representatives about the situation where fire was opened on themselves, that is, on those UN representatives, and if so, what did they tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well one rather drastic example of a killing of a French soldier. I saw this picture for the first time on the media, on television, and it represented -- what was broadcast was the exact moment when the French soldier was killed and him falling off an engineer's vehicle while he was trying to -- as he was trying to set up some containers in front of Holiday Inn. And the first reaction, when I saw that image on television, was that, again, something has been set up because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you here. I'm sorry. Can you tell us why, first of all -- why do you say "again," and what is your impression based Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18608 to 18620. on in relation to the setup?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was almost impossible for any reasonable person that the videocamera can be switched on and waiting for a bullet to hit a person. Unless this was prepared beforehand and announced in some way. When I said "again" is related to some previous setups, for instance, like that one in Vasa Miskin Street where what existed for a long time among the population of Sarajevo, if in some place you see a camera, you have to run as fast as you can from that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. What can you tell us about this incident about the firing position and the direction of fire, that is, of the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was during one very short time, the same day when the soldier was killed, two groups arrived in Lukavica in order to conduct an investigation about firing from our side, by our side, towards this soldier. And one group was made up of French officers from the sector command, and the second group was sent by General Rose personally, and this second group was led by his adjutant or his chief of staff, Michael Stanley. From both groups separately -- or with both groups, I went to Grbavica, and it was on their request, because there was a possible direction of fire that there was a red building where the Invest Banka was, that was denoted as the possible source of fire. So it was together with them that I visited all the premises of that red building, and no traces of any firing was found, not only firing but even presence of any persons in that building which in the direction -- looking towards where the incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you remind us, who was given the blame, the responsibility, by international institutions for this killing of a French soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although my understanding after I visited the premises with these two groups, I understood from their report that the Serb side was not to blame for this incident; it was already after a few days that it was officially publicised from the command that it was the Serb side who was to blame for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe this is a perfect moment for this cassette to be shown, if I have your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution submits that still no proper basis has been laid for the showing of the video. The witness has given evidence as to what he knows. Showing the video takes it no further. That is not the way to get in that evidence. The Defence could have taken steps to call the individual who appears in the video. They admit they have not done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just ask one question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You've talked to us about an interview in the magazine that you read. The photograph of the person, of Mr. Garaplija, was this magazine published in the article? The photograph of the person, of Mr. Garaplija, was this photograph published in the article?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you see this person, would it be possible for you to recognise this person on the video?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, I think it is useful to know if the witness can recognise this person who might be subpoenaed by your -- or summoned by your Chamber to appear as an important potential witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it is about whether Mr. Garaplija in the interview is the same as the picture of Mr. Garaplija the witness has seen in a newspaper, I think either a still or a silent playing of the video would perfectly serve that purpose, I would say. And I would see no objection against -- for these purposes to play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just the point that I raised. But I believe that the video without the text doesn't seem to be very informative for your Chamber, and your Chamber must learn what happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that's a different matter. That's a different matter. The question of admission of this video and the transcript into evidence is a different one from what you just told us. You just asked the witness whether he would think that he could recognise that person. So if that's the issue, there is a perfect solution for that. But that's a totally different matter. If you think that the Chamber should know the content of the video, then we have I would say a totally different procedural issue, and that is in what way to introduce that video. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is another point. It is useful to know if the content of what we hope is a future witness, what he said on this tape, and it is in conformity with what the witness -- this witness was able to read in the press and other sources. Now, not giving us the leave to demonstrate this and to inform you of this, that is refusing the truth. But if you're refusing the truth, that's very well. We can refuse the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a conclusion, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that by not accepting in this procedural way the video, that that would be denying the truth, as I told you before, the Chamber will have to consider whether there is an acceptable procedural way to know the content of the video. A different matter is whether this witness should be confronted with it. Those are two totally different matters. I would first like to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go on to another subject. We can make the observation that the Defence wanted to hear the witness confirm the truthfulness of what he heard in what the Defence tried to demonstrate. But again, this was refused by the Chamber to the Defence, and here the rights of the Defence have been offended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber will consider the matter. That's the only thing I said. I did not immediately grant leave to confront this witness with the content of the video. That's the only thing that happened until now.
