I take it that we'll consider it during the next break which would be the most -- and perhaps during the last, unless there's anything the Prosecution would add to the -- to what has been said until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I could add something in the absence of the witness, rather than waste time now, at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that just before the break. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can we now please go back to other elements. First of all, in order to save time, can you tell us, yes or no, whether there were military courts that were established during the war on the side of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let us focus on the problem of your relations with UN officials. How many officials did you meet in the course of your activities in the PTT building? Of course, I'm not asking for a specific number; just a general estimate of how many of them did you meet.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be precise, can you tell me, you meanwhile I was in the PTT building or throughout my duty when I was the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I mean the entire period.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will not err if I say certainly over a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name of Mr. Patrick Henneberry mean anything to you? What I mean is, was this person one of your friends? Did you have brotherly exchanges, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am very sorry. This name vaguely rings a bell, but I cannot remember who this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase my question. Was this one of your close friends with whom you may have gone and taken -- had meals together or had drinks, or you shared some emotions together, something like that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not, otherwise I would have remembered who this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now can we speak about the strategy, if you know about the general strategy, of the SRK. Do you know if there was a plan on the level of the army and that this plan had the objective of completely eliminating Muslim population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of any such plan. I don't think anyone could have devised such a plan because it's simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move on to the subject of shelling, the shelling of areas of Sarajevo. My first question: Do you know if the -- there were military targets in the hands of the enemy inside Sarajevo? Any military targets?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH army had its general staff in Sarajevo, the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show a map to the witness, a map that we showed yesterday to another witness. I would like to have it again. I don't know if there are any markings on the map. Before we show it to the witness, Mr. President, in order to save time, my intention is to show the map to the witness and then ask him if he thinks that the information contained therein is accurate. If there's anything to be added or taken off. But it's up to you, Mr. President. I thought this was just suitable for the purpose of saving time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I recall at least one occasion in the Prosecution case where such a course was vigorously opposed by the Defence. I have not been informed of this proposal. I have no idea what the map is, but even so if I am shown the map, I may allow it. If we could just have access to it and be informed, perhaps on a piece of paper in English, so the witness doesn't hear it, who it is that marked the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a very uncommon way of -- because whether the marking is complete depends on the questions put to the witness who marked. We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I withdraw. But there will be a very long list -- we will have a very long list, I'm afraid, in this respect. I am very surprised to hear that the Prosecution is not informed, not aware of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there any military targets that you were aware of in Sarajevo, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the time you claimed I said in the beginning that also because the witness would like to leave, that the parties should be very precise in keeping the time. So therefore, use your time as you deem fit. At the same time, I don't know whether this would be the only source, but to ask one witness to correct the work of another witness is not the way --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know, yes or no, what the situation was involving military targets inside the city of Sarajevo more or less?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in charge of working on the map. It was not part of my assignment. But I know something in respect of certain military facilities. My knowledge, however, is more focussed to the existence of military units in Sarajevo, not their locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What can you tell us about the Ciglane tunnel? Were there any targets there; and if yes, what? What were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ciglane area, there are two tunnels. One is used for regular traffic, and the other is not finished, was not finished. And the Muslim side kept some of its weaponry there, and according to what I know, there were two tanks there for sure, and a mortar mounted on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to my initial question, that of the shelling of the town. When you have military targets located on the ground floor -- strike that. Let me rephrase the question. In your capacity of a senior officer, are you in the position to know that the use of a particular weapon is legitimate or not in view of the overall circumstances? Yes or no. In principle.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. In your capacity of a military officer, are you able to tell in light of the circumstances whether the use of a particular weapon is legitimate or not, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I am able to reach a conclusion to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When we have military targets located on ground floor or on the first floor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There is no basis established with this witness, no sufficient basis, for him to offer such opinions. A liaison officer who has himself said he was outside the command and control in relation to what one might call the fighting forces, with a background in training in intelligence, languages, is stretching it, if I could use the vernacular, too far. I might add that we have heard evidence, I think, from a number of witnesses who had some better basis of qualification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, it has been asked to many witnesses, even those who might not have been experts in the law of warfare. I'll allow you to put the question, and the Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Later weigh the evidence presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you have military targets on ground floor or on first floor in a building that you cannot see or hit with direct fire and you want to target it, you want to hit it, what is the type of weapon that you would use in order to open fire on this type of target?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the targeting is legitimate, then I would use artillery weapons for indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What weapons precisely do you have in mind when you say "indirect fire" weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to the artillery weapons with a specified incoming trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of any such artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All types of artillery pieces that have this type of -- or that use this type of incoming trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Am I right in assuming that you are referring to mortars or Howitzers when they are used from this position and in this position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell us, please, brigade commanders, did they have artillery pieces? Did they have them at their disposal, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of establishment, every brigade has an artillery group, a brigade artillery group. And brigades differ in this respect, depending on how strong they were in terms of troops and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as firing itself is concerned, who must issue an order? And I'm speaking of these artillery pieces. Who is in charge of issuing such an order to open fire?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are still talking about a brigade, the use of a brigade artillery group is within the province of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would such an order leave any traces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it needn't be in written form, but any activity by a brigade, as I have already indicated, must be reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But was your answer yes or no? Would such an order leave any traces of its existence? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be traces, so to speak, in a report that is submitted thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If such an order is issued in terms of brigade artillery, would it leave any paper trail later on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move -- actually, let us go back to the issue of shelling of military targets inside the town using indirect fire artillery pieces. What can you tell us about the margin of error in the use of such artillery pieces, if you know? Errors in terms of targeting.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of artillery weapons, appropriate observing and correction of fire is always done before opening fire. However, I must say that it is never very precise, and very rarely does the first shell hit the target, which tells you clearly how frequent such errors are, not only that they are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you now tell us something about the issue of mixed commissions. We have heard a number of things concerning these commissions, but what can you tell us about the willingness of the Serb side to establish such joint or mixed commissions and how they functioned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to clarify the terminology, let me just reiterate that at the lower level, at the level of lower staffs, there were mixed working groups. However, when it comes to the corps level, we had mixed commissions. These mix commissioned discussed at their meetings the issues with the purpose of putting an end to hostilities and finding a peaceful solution to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the witness to be shown an exhibit, 453, please. I think we have some handwritten remarks on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you please focus on item 3 (c). That is, the last portion of the first page in the Serbian language. Tell us when you have looked at it, and also please pay attention to the signature. Have you read it, the relevant portion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. First question: Do you recognise the form of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's a regular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the signature? Are you able to identify it? Have you already seen this handwritten signature?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot identify the person who signed the document because the word "Za" meaning "for" precedes the name. So somebody else signed the document for Dragomir Milosevic. Probably the duty operative officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was that customary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Speaking of section (c), that is item 3 (c), can you just confirm the contents of this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the basis of this section alone. I cannot remember the first part, that is, the meeting which was convened at the airport. I don't recall this particular meeting. However, the remaining items, yes, I can confirm them. I'm aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we're talking about commissions, do you know, what does the name of Markale make you think of? Does it ring a bell? I suppose it does. No, no, no, it has got nothing to do with the document, Witness. It's a general question. Does it sound familiar, the name of Markale?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In a nutshell, if you can just briefly tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Markale?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a resident of Sarajevo, I am aware of the Markale market, that is, I have been aware of this market ever since I was a little child. It is the largest market inside the town of Sarajevo. From the war, however, it is the name of the location where one of the greatest tragedies occurred during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We will address the issue of the commission and the incident in question. You have the document to your right. And please, tell us, first of all, did you ever receive any protest concerning item 3(c)?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now move on to the issue of commissions, in particular, the commissions that dealt with the issue of shelling. Do you know if the Serb side wanted or showed willingness to establish a joint or mixed commissions in order to establish what had happened in particular incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the corps command, there was readiness to act in case of even a smallest incident in order to have the incident investigated with the representatives of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was that the case of the Markale market as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Markale market incident received a much stronger response, of course. And I remember that within a brief period of time, the main staff issued an order to establish a mixed commission who would investigate the incident at the very site. And I think that Colonel Lugonja and Colonel Cvetkovic, who was an artillery man, were appointed members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military hierarchy reacted, intervened, immediately in order to verify at the level of the brigade, in terms of territory, if fire had indeed been opened?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that as part of this order which was issued by the main staff, it was directed that every single barrel should be inspected in order to establish where the fire had been opened from our positions. Whether I say every single barrel, I don't mean only the inspection of the relevant artillery pieces, but also to interview the crews manning these artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: According to what you know, was that indeed done?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see who could have refused such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So I take your answer to mean yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, when do you intend to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this question about the break should entail an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was a leading question and one which purported to be based on the previous question but it was not. The witness made a presumption that the order had been complied with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I refer, of course, to the question "so I take your answer to mean yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's at least an interpretation of the answer. But the examination is interrupted anyhow. I'd first like to ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom so that we can deal with the matters remaining for the next three minutes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I have just had a glance on the document. And Mr. Ierace, it appears that one of the subjects of the interview of this third party relates closely to an incident described by the witness during his testimony. Starting from that point of view, I'd like to hear briefly from the parties, and perhaps first hear your objection, if there would be any remaining objection. And then hear from the Defence, but just as briefly as possible, what we -- not only on whether you object or not, but also on what we preferably should do under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, there is no proper basis established for this interview to become part of the evidence, which is clearly the intention of the Defence. It would seem there is no comment that could be made by the witness, none is apparent at this stage. It is simply led, in effect, as corroboration of the hearsay he has already given. A relevant factor is that according to the witness, the incident sparked an investigation by General Rose. We know the Defence has had this tape in its possession since before General Rose gave evidence, they have had it in their possession since December 2001. No questions pertaining to the investigation were put to him. The Defence has admitted that it has made no attempt to have the alleged confessor brought before the Court. There is simply no basis upon which this video can be admitted into evidence. It certainly sounds very interesting, but the way to do it is to call the person who is allegedly giving this information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the historical background shows us that it is your [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was about to change to the French channel. I missed part of what you said, at least -- perhaps because you were talking at such a low voice that the interpreters could not hear you. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said simply historically, the responsibility shall be yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'd like to have an answer on the procedural issue raised by Mr. -- And -- by Mr. Ierace. No. Let me be quite clear: The way the Chamber is handling this problem, and as I indicated -- I indicated that before, that it might be of importance for the Chamber to see this evidence and to hear the evidence this witness could add to what he has told us already about this incident. At the same time, the Chamber should keep the procedural standards such that both parties will have an opportunity to present their case properly. But just referring to whether history will tell you whether the Chamber is right in a decision it has not taken yet, I'm seeking argument to be exchanged so that the Chamber can give a proper decision where it has showed clearly that the information contained in this evidence might be of importance. So therefore, I invite you again to respond to what Mr. Ierace said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ierace has -- is right, perfectly right, when he says and only when he says that this is certainly interesting. Second, I don't see any link with Mr. Rose. We can ask questions to whomever we want or like, and it is impossible to ask questions in respect of everything in cases of individual witnesses. Third, this witness, and you indicated justly so, that this witness was talking about a significant incident in terms of manipulations. And it is the position of the Defence that we have to say -- hold on a second, we have to be very cautious, very prudent when it comes to the manipulations. And here, we have the possibility of listening to the experience of a person who was a BH army sniper who knew about the activities of these -- this group. And I think it is imperative that we deal here more with the substance than with the form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please also respond to the suggestion Mr. Ierace, that the best way of dealing with the matter would be to call the witness who gave the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that this is not the best way. This is an additional way, and very interesting. Why is that? Because according to what you would be able to see, Mr. President, you would be in a position perhaps to ask certain questions of the witness, although you probably would not be able to do it seeing the way that things are progressing now if we have to wait for a possible summoning of the last witness mentioned, this person, Mr. Garaplija. Although it is certain as far as we are concerned that he will not come bearing in mind what he might testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I have a question for Mr. Ierace. Mr. Ierace, your objection goes to procedural matters or to the substance of the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Your Honour, I haven't had an opportunity yet to read the transcript. I've glanced at it. I would be grateful for that opportunity before I responded in terms of the substance. For example, I wish to establish in my own mind whether this is hearsay, and if so whether it is double hearsay, and whether this is the person who claims to have shot the French soldier. I think that's important as to whether is material should go in. So it's both. And I might add in relation to the procedure this does not seem to be one of those cases where when General Rose gave his evidence the Defence could not have known about this investigation. It would seem that surely the accused would have known, the accused was here, and he could have told the Defence about this incident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: As far as I understand, this tape was disclosed by the Prosecution as exculpatory evidence. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We disclose evidence under two relevant categories in relation to this type of material: Evidence which may be exculpatory, and because it is a reciprocal disclosure trial, evidence which may be of assistance to the Defence in presenting their Defence. And on that basis, we disclosed the material. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So this tape could be exculpatory?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The tape in itself may be, because it's disclosed under those conditions. But more importantly, it may enable the Defence to make further inquiries so they could then be in a position to call first-hand evidence, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter during the break. We'll adjourn until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter of the video and the transcript. First of all, the Chamber expresses that it would have been the proper way of introducing this evidence by calling the relevant witnesses, not necessarily Mr. Garaplija, but perhaps even Mr. Herenda [phoen] or Mr. Bozic or whoever is mentioned in there. That certainly would have assisted the Chamber in better appreciating such evidence. By not doing this or not taking any initiative, timely, in order to achieve this, the Defence has taken a considerable risk that these witnesses could not be heard any more, whereas they might have been of importance for the presentation of the Defence case. And the Chamber has also considered that the Defence should give some thought on whether they would try to still call these witnesses or one of these witnesses in order to achieve the best that can be achieved in this respect. In the present situation, the Chamber is very much concerned to find out exactly what is the personal knowledge of the present witness, and therefore the Chamber will put a few questions to the witness before it will allow the Defence to play the video and to put questions to the witness. There is not much time left, then, for the Defence, if my time keeping is correct. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Indic, I would like to ask you some further questions in respect of the incident in which a French soldier died. Could you tell us from whom you first learned about the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first information in relation to the incident came from the TV. It was the recording that I saw on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just told us that the presence of the TV was raising some suspicion. Did the television show the French soldier first alive and then being shot? Where did the report start? At what moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the recording, you can see a vehicle. It's a vehicle, a forklift. It was supposed to lift the containers, and there was a soldier who was in the bulletproof jacket and a helmet. He was driving this vehicle by himself. Then at the next moment you saw a French soldier falling off the vehicle on the right-hand side. He was going in the direction of Grbavica. Behind him was the Holiday Inn hotel. And he fell to the right in the direction of the museum. So you can see the moment the soldier was shot, and you can see his activity prior to him being shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that broadcast the same day the event happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was publicly broadcasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you then get further information about the incident, apart from what you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, what followed was an investigation, as I said, conducted by two teams of United Nations. The French team and the team of General Rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My conclusion following my visit with these two teams, my conclusion was that they were convinced that the incident was not caused by the Serb side. But I believe it was already two days later that the main staff the Army of Republika Srpska was informed and blamed, saying that the incident was caused by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that your forces were blamed for having perpetrated this killing, whereas no signs had been found during your investigation initiated by General Rose that the shot would have come from your side. Do you know who perpetrated this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have told you, by reading the interview in the Slobodna Bosna magazine, I found out that the -- this was done by members of the Seva unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have any other source that would confirm that these individuals were responsible for this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to make it sure, your knowledge about how the event happened you learned that from television. Your knowledge as to your forces not being responsible you learned from the investigation that was initiated by General Rose. And you took an active part in that. And what you know about who did perpetrate, it's exclusively on the basis of the newspaper interview that you obtained knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the video may be shown. You may put questions to the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Of course, within the limit of the answers the witness has just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I thank the booth, particularly the English booth, if they can interpret what is heard on the video because the tape is both in Serbian and in English. However, occasionally of very poor quality in terms of audio. Thank you. We can show the video. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the number of the exhibit. For the transcript, 1841.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we play it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. Could we stop playing the video, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, for the record, I'm told that this was not on the exhibit list. In the circumstances, I don't oppose it being added, although no leave was sought. And it seems that the entire video is to be played, not the three excerpts which were provided to the Prosecution by the Defence last week. I simply state that for the record, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is not at all the entire video. It's just the excerpt which is of interest for us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that Mr. Ierace said that you should play the entire video if you want to rely on these parts. Is that correct, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we were given three segments approximately 2 minutes each. I gather that instead of playing three segments, the Defence now proposes to play one large segment. I don't know if that goes beyond the three segments that we were given. Perhaps that could be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I said this is just an excerpt which interests us. It's only 2 minutes long. And it is only this that we are interested in. It is true that the Prosecution also received other excerpts, but we are not asking for the viewing of those. It's just this excerpt, which is given to the booth and to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... With the translation, or do we hear English on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation booths, I believe, do have the copies of the transcript since yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, could the video be restarted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel indicate which page this begins at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the English booth, we will start from page 87 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The next sniping activity I would describe as firing by a soldier. The soldier was a member of the United Nations forces. I think he was of French origin. And the idea behind the action was -- SPEAKER: The Serbian side or -- SPEAKER: The soldier was hit from across, from across the way opposite, opposite the Holiday Inn not far from the building of the executive council. SPEAKER: From across the way opposite the Holiday Inn hotel. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] Near the building of the executive council. SPEAKER: Executive council. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] On an empty space on the crossroads, there is the building of the museum. SPEAKER: Museum. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] While the street. SPEAKER: While the street. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] The street leads to the valley of Miljacka River to Grbavica. SPEAKER: Leads to the valley of the Miljacka River to Grbavica. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] And Grbavica was controlled by Serb forces. SPEAKER: And Grbavica was controlled by Serb forces. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] However, Herenda [phoen] And Bozic. SPEAKER: Herenda And Bozic. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] I think it was Dragan Bozic, and with a third person, I cannot remember his name, from Seva. SPEAKER: I cannot remember his name. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] He climbed onto the building of the Executive Council. SPEAKER: Building of the Executive Council. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] Which was located in the direction I described. SPEAKER: Located in the direction I described. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] And from there he used a sniper rifle. SPEAKER: From there he used a sniper rifle. SPEAKER: [Interpretation] To shoot the soldier. SPEAKER: To shoot the soldier."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, very briefly now, do you have knowledge of other incidents that would have been comparable to the one that we just heard about on this tape? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly which ones?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first killing of the UN soldier in Sarajevo area occurred near the Sarajevo airport. It was in the southern side that there is an access road towards the Sarajevo airport from a place called Kotorac. Muslim soldiers opened fire from the area of Butmir. And on that occasion, two French soldiers were killed. The misuse of these killings, I can see in the fact that I don't know for what reasons, the monument to these two soldiers was set up, was erected, on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the discussions with UN members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. The witness has again been invited with no qualification as to how he knows of these things to tell us of what he's aware. And that is an improper way, in my respectful submission, for evidence to be elicited in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, when you are responding to questions of Mr. Piletta-Zanin concerning this second incident, same questions: How did you learn about them? How did you learn about this second incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned it from members of the French battalion who were stationed at the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they ever identify who fired at the soldier that was, if I understand you well, killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was ascertained, and it was known from the very beginning because the French had one armoured vehicle located at the entrance to the airport, which was an observation point. It was from the very beginning, there was no dilemma, that the fire was opened from Butmir, from the area under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would say that the fire came from the BiH-controlled area. Was it ever identified who fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the confusion you create is that you're referring to an incident of which from different sources some at first unknown to the witness, others only known by watching television, and a third category is where other people say who performed that without any knowledge of the witness. If you refer to similar incidents, it's highly confusing, and it's suggestive. And what we would like to know is what the witness knows rather than what is unclearly suggested to him and where we get whatever response to such suggestions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, presumably you know this, and you can tell us, how do you know this? Would you please be able to tell us what do you know, if you know, about the Seva group that we spoke of earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony so far, I told you what I know about this group. It's a special unit which is supposed to do special tasks. And special tasks, first of all, what I mean is elimination of persons, killing of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You have spoken about elimination. According to your knowledge and as far as you know, was there a strategy that was used? What I mean is was there a frequency of action like the one that we saw described on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say decisively that this was part of the strategy of the other side. But I do know that there was much talk of operations of this unit. That was directed against its own population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The person that we saw earlier, that is, Mr. Garaplija, do you know a person who knows this person?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the whole leadership would know it, of the AID would know it, the Agency for Information and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A couple of questions before finishing. You have spoken to us about the airport. I'm going to change the subject. I'd like to know, what can you tell about the corridors?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise in your question. Are you referring to the blue roads, the humanitarian corridors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there any open corridors, corridors that would have been opened for civilians, if so, when and how often they were opened and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a result of one of the agreements which was designed to facilitate life for the residents of Sarajevo, a number of so-called blue roads were opened. They went across the Sarajevo airport and further on, Dobrinja, Butmir, Lukavica, and Ilidza, via the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge on the axis Grbavica, part of the Sarajevo and for a brief period of time, there was -- via Vogosca, Visoko, and further on towards central Bosnia. Those blue roads in principle functioned daily within the limited period of time in the morning and in the afternoon. There were points, crossing points from one territory to the other which were manned by the so-called controllers whose tasks was not to control the individuals but to see to it that the humanitarian convoys did not carry any weapons and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General Galic, did he take part in the establishment of these corridors? We are approaching the end of your testimony. And second, what can you tell us, provided that you know something, about the personality of General Galic when it comes to these humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the immediate participation of the corps commander in the implementation of the blue roads project, I can say that his word was the final one because he issued orders to the brigades whose areas of responsibility were near the access of the blue records in order to ensure an unhindered functioning of these communication lines. As for the -- for your second question, that is, the attitude of General Galic with respect to the humanitarian issues, I can say briefly that it was always my impression of General Galic as a professional soldier, professional in terms of everything that is understood by a military vocation which also involves such an attitude towards humanitarian issue which is -- which was always positive as far as General Galic is concerned. And he always had a very clear and decisive attitude when it comes to combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. This concludes my examination of the witness, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to begin the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I say something in that regard in the absence of the witness and in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is necessary to do it right at this moment? Yes, then I would like to ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom and turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, we are informed that for certain reasons, you'd like to go back to where you come from not after the weekend but before the weekend. Could you give us some indication on what exactly is of importance for you to go back? We're trying to manage, but we'll have to see whether we are able to do so. I understood that there was something on Sunday you'd like to attend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the plane -- the Banja Luka/Belgrade plane leaves on Sunday, and I have to be at work on Monday. My arrival here was planned for the 18th. The plan had already had been made in advance. And one could not assume that I would have to stay this long, specifically if Your Honour wishes to know what it is all about, I have to be present at the yearly analysis of the work that has been done in my company. And I am not the only person participating in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that starts on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see whether we can use the time in such a way -- we try to have you back in time. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it's of any use, I am available this afternoon and on Saturday. I don't have any commitments, any other commitments here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And your flight is on Sunday, I do understand? We could see what could be done either today or tomorrow. We could investigate that. I don't know whether there's any courtroom available or any supporting staff available. But let's just start now. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indic, as I understand the evidence that you have given us so far, especially in terms of your liaison duties, you were a conduit for information passing from the army of which you were a member to other parties, including the UN. Is that correct? Would you agree with that summary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including also the information coming from them and addressed to my army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from those duties, you also acted as an interpreter from time to time for various senior officers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and, indeed, in the VRS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree with your description of them being senior officers. I always helped with interpretation regardless of the level involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have also told us that, as I understand it, you had absolutely no power to make decisions, that your work obligations were confined to simply liaison, as I have described it, and interpretation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. I object as to the expression "as I have described it" in view of the precision provided by the witness. I think the Prosecution cannot continue this line of questioning because the issue has been clarified and corrected by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I don't know whether it's my recollection that the witness had in no respect any power for decisions. But could you please try to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw. I withdraw the objection in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall yesterday that you told us that you did not have the power to make decisions in relation to the passage of humanitarian convoys or in relation to protests, that these matters were simply passed through you to others for decisions to be made? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We clarified that previously, I did not have any authorisation to reach decisions on my own concerning the movement of humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And apart from that, you did not have any power to make decisions in relation to protests, did you? You simply passed them on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single protest was intended and sent out to the group for cooperation with UNPROFOR as a final addressee. The group in question did not have authority to make any decisions regarding these protests. They were supposed to forward these protests to their original addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were a member of that group, you tell us, the liaison group. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, what rank were you in February of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February of 1992, I held the rank of Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When were you promoted after that position, after that rank? When were you next promoted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first next rank that I had, that of a major, I got in July 1992 as a regular promotion because I had passed the examination, the relevant examination to become a major previously that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was the next promotion after July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the next promotion in 1995. I was promoted to the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel, which was a temporary promotion. I had been given that promotion six months earlier than normal, than regular promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. When in 1995 were you promoted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was promoted by virtue of a general staff decision adopted in January 1995. However, in order to avoid confusion, we, as former officers of the JNA, we were also members of the 30th Human Resources Centre. And the order coming from that centre came sometime in July that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you say that you were promoted by virtue of a general staff decision adopted in January of 1995? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, page 79, line 9, not temporary promotion but an early promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did your duties differ at all between August of 1994 and January of 1995 from what they were before August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This period falls outside the relevant times. The question refers to the period between August 1994 and January 1995. I don't know whether I have to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness has raised this issue, let me take the opportunity to object. We formally object because the question falls outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is denied. So you may answer the question, but you may do that tomorrow because it's a quarter to 2.00 now, and we have to stop. So tomorrow, you may tell us whether your duties changed in August 1994 from what they were before up until January 1995. The parties should be prepared for any additional hearing. We'll first of course have to investigate whether it will be possible to hear for more time either today or tomorrow. They should keep themselves available for any message from the registry. If there's any reason why the parties could not appear this afternoon or tomorrow, I'd like to hear about it. And similarly, I'd like hear from General Galic if there would be any objection apart from the strain it will put on your health.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, there is. Preceding what you said at the very beginning of this hearing, it is our mission now to address a number of issues to the Canadian authorities in respect of a witness that you know about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's not do this in the presence of the witness. Mr. Usher, could I first ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Would you please keep yourself available today and tomorrow also outside the hours indicated to you. I do understand that you understand my English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you still have work to be done on the issue we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's not just a little work. The Canadian administration want us to give them a very detailed list of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I did understand that you were willing to provide this list today, so that means that it will certainly take you a couple of hours because -- therefore, some time, but now I'm taking into consideration two days might still be left. And if we have to prioritise, we'll have to see how to do it. But I am aware, and you have drawn my attention to the fact, that you need considerable time to prepare a response for the Canadian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second, my flight tomorrow is at 4.00 or 4.30. And I simply have to be in Geneva because of a meeting tomorrow night. So the best solution for me would be if the Prosecution could make an effort to speed up the examination and to focus directly on the essential --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am trying to solve a problem, and I am not seeking the advice of the parties for what the other party should do to solve the problem. Both parties should make themselves available for today and tomorrow. We'll try to take into account the problems you have. The Defence team exists of two persons. They might consider to split up some of the work. And we'll consider the matter. First, practical thing I have to do, to see whether there's any courtroom available. We will adjourn until tomorrow unless the parties receive a message that we would spend some time this afternoon as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case, because it's not clear whether this is a continuation of this morning's session or a new session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, are you ready to continue the cross-examination? Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Before we start, I'd like to thank you for finding a courtroom. I wanted to say that there were a few things exchanged in English, and this exchange occurred in the presence of the witness who understands English perfectly well. The Prosecution is aware of this, and I am surprised to see that the Prosecution allowed it to express itself like this. Because we've spoken about General Galic and about speaking in Serb to him. I don't think the Prosecution should speak in English in front of the witness if the witness can understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please respond as briefly as possible, I'm not very much inclined to spend more time on procedural issues that are not of such an urgent character that they could not be dealt with after the witness has been examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, nothing was said of any significance or importance to the witness between myself and other members of the legal team. I'm surprised to hear the complaint. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is one -- I think the parties should refrain from loudly discussing whatever in the presence of a witness. That's number 1. There is at least a difference, then, if Mr. Piletta-Zanin is there that he understands some English, but parties should refrain from doing it. Otherwise, we will have to ask the witness next time to stay out of the courtroom, and that takes time as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Indic, I asked you generally whether your duties between August 1994 and January 1995 differed from those you carried out before August 1994. What is the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you act as an interpreter in languages other than English?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I don't know any other foreign languages. I only know English as a foreign language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many officer in the barracks building at Lukavica in the relevant period other than you, spoke English? That is, officers based in those barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them in the barracks spoke English, but I do know how many in my group for cooperating with UNPROFOR spoke English. It was myself and Mr. Luledzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was he based in the PTT building or in the Lukavica headquarters with you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At different times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At different times, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Him aside, how many other officers based in the Lukavica headquarters other than you from the time that you moved to the Lukavica headquarters until August 1994 spoke English well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President. The question is not precise. I would be -- I would appreciate it if the witness could leave. This has to do with the precision that is necessary for the question. We know that there were other officers in Lukavica than those that Mr. Ierace is thinking of. Perhaps he could clarify his question because there were various officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would have thought that was obvious, Mr. President. I'm happy to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it took you five lines for something that would have needed half a line, one line, not more than one and a half line. We have now been confronted with these time constraints again and again. I urge the parties not to interfere unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Lest there be any doubt, Mr. Indic, I mean talking about officers and other members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps who were based in those headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many officers in the Lukavica command spoke a foreign language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, did you know anyone who spoke English whilst you were stationed at Lukavica headquarters up until August of 1994? And I mean apart from other members of your liaison group.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that some people studied foreign languages in the course of their education, but I didn't speak to anyone from the command in the English language. So it's not possible for me to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did you know anyone, apart from yourself, in the SRK who spoke English, leaving assumptions aside?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a certain period of time, when the humanitarian corridors by the Sarajevo airport were opened, part of the group for securing air flights was formed. Two air officers, liaison air officers were made responsible for this. Major Branko Milosevic who spoke English, and Sunka, Slobodan, a warrant officer. As far as I know, he did not speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were they both members of your liaison group?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't members of the liaison group that I belonged to. They were air force officers responsible for liaising, and they were connected to the chief of the air force department in the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long was Branko Milosevic at the Lukavica headquarters for? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Milosevic wasn't in the command in Lukavica. As an air force officer for liaising, he was at the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll repeat the question. I'm asking you officers who were based at the Lukavica headquarters. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked how many officers from Lukavica command spoke a foreign language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I asked you do you know -- did you know any officers at the headquarters when you were there who spoke English. Mr. Indic, it's a very simple question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat this: I don't know who spoke English in the Lukavica command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the liaison officers in the PTT when it was started up again have to speak English, that is, the Bosnian Serb liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people whose duties it was to liaise in the PTT building did speak English, but these people were not professional officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Because we don't have much time, a yes would have sufficed as an answer to that question, if you follow me. Now, your boss in 1992 and early 1993, was your immediate boss Colonel Zarkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he speak English?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he leave in May 1993 and go to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which month, but in 1993, he did go to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to represent him as chief of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For what period of time did that last?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted until he returned to the same duties from the Ministry of Defence. I don't remember when that was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What year was it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It was after August of 1994, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does that mean that in his absence, the other members of your liaison group reported to you and that you gave them directions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us a few times during your evidence in chief that you were one of a group, but it seems that for some indeterminate period from mid-1993 onwards, you were more equal than them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I be provided with the exact quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that Mr. Ierace is referring to any statement. In the evidence in chief that he belonged to a group... If you would have a source, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not at the moment, without LiveNote, Mr. President. I'll see if we can struggle through, perhaps come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is it contested that the witness testified several times that he was part of a group?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what surprises me is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what surprises you. I'm asking you whether it is contested that the witness said several times that he belonged and that he functioned in a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then would you like to have the source for?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's what I wanted to tell you a minute ago so as not to waste time. As the expression, you are more equal than them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that's a conclusion that is put by Mr. Ierace to the witness, and it has got nothing to do with the quote. That's what was my first thought as well. And please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us that in 1981 -- I withdraw that. Did Colonel Zarkovic come back to the SRK at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Into the same position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is there any reason as to why you cannot remember even approximately the year that he returned to become your boss again?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is. The time that has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether when he returned, General Galic was still the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidentally, has Colonel Zarkovic retired from the army of RS, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about his details. I don't know when he retired, but I do know that he is now a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And as such, he receives a pension from the government of Republika Srpska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask him about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Also, you used the word "pensioner." One might reasonably assume that if he's retired, and you tell us that he is a pensioner, he would receive a pension as a result of his service with the Army of Republika Srpska. In that case, if for whatever reason the authorities wished to contact Colonel Zarkovic, you would expect them to have his details, including his address, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I can only make assumptions, but I don't know whether they have his address or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me why you are so reticent to make such a simple assumption as that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not at all reticent. I'm just telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was the last time that you saw General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think I saw him about a month ago while passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know his address?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see what the relevance of the -- of this person's address is with regard to the case that we have to assess today. I'm wondering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you're inviting me to indicate the relevance, I think in the interests of the Defence, I would have to do it in private session in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be a possibility to deal with the issue, let's say tomorrow in the beginning of the next session, and you move to your next subject now. But I would like to tell you already now, Mr. Ierace, that the witness is not in a position that he has to explain why he doesn't follow you in assuming certain facts. You have asked the witness about facts but he needs not explain why he does not follow assumptions that might be true, might not be true. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever carry out interpreting duties for General Mladic in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection with regard to the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, if you wish to hear me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's apparent that it might be relevant. It cannot be said it's less relevant. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acted as interpreter at the meetings that General Mladic attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's between September 1992 and August 1994. Is that correct, including that period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions when these meetings were held. Perhaps on five occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he sometimes attend the mixed military working groups?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it was necessary to sign one of the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But General Mladic spoke English, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he speaks English, but he never spoke English in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I see. And did you interpret for any other generals in the general staff or, as I think it was called then, the supreme staff, in the relevant period, I should add?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never called the supreme staff. It was called the general staff. And I interpreted when it was necessary at all the meetings. And to be more specific, this includes the meetings that General Milovanovic had, some of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And General Tolimir, was he another one?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also interpreted at meetings of the mixed military working group at the Sarajevo airport, and General Tolimir was present there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was his particular area of responsibility? Did it have anything to do with intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was deputy chief of the general staff for intelligence affairs in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you attended an intelligence course, you completed it in 1986. How long did that take?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, before I answer. I have something to change. I said General Tolimir was deputy chief of the staff for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is at page 10, line 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Missing a reference to "and security."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long did that course take, the intelligence course?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And for how long did you study foreign languages in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For ten and a half months in Belgrade in the JNA school of foreign languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that you're an intelligent man. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult for one to speak of one's self. If that's what you believe, then I hope that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And certainly, the job that you did in that period between September 1992 and August 1994 involved a considerable degree of trust on the part of the senior leadership of the VRS, trust of you. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust is a basis for the functioning of an army, mutual trust among officers, between superiors and subordinates. I don't think trust in my regard was in any way different from the general principle of trust that prevailed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, they trusted you with their words. General Mladic trusted you with his words when he dealt with the warring parties and the United Nations, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an interpreter, it was my duty to interpret literally, to interpret what was said literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And they chose you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As did General Galic, he trusted you to communicate accurately for him with various United Nations organisations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They depended on you, they trusted you also, because inevitably, they wanted you to keep their confidence, I suggest to you, mixing as you did with the leadership of the VRS and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that inevitably in the work you did, the work that you tell us you did, you would be expected to keep confidences in relation to the people for whom you interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's taken for granted. Even your interpreters who are here, it's their duty to be confidential and to keep what they interpret secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you told us before the break, correct me if I'm wrong, I haven't checked it, that there was some sort of acceleration of your promotion to Lieutenant-Colonel, I think you said, by some six months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you think perhaps that reflected, given the level at which that decision was taken to promote you, considerable satisfaction on their part with the job you did, the trust they held in you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I performed my duties professionally, and that was a way of awarding me for having professionally carried out my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think the point is made, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the structure of your duties, was there an order given on the 7th of February, 1993, by the general command as to the responsibilities of the liaison group?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This morning, you were asked questions about an order dated the 6th of August, 1993, which you said referred to your obligations. Did that order change those obligations from what they were before that date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDIC [Resumed]
